question: Why is this a plan, not an opportunistic patch bundled into other work?
answer: Because the four wins in F001 + Ruff S in F002 + actions pinning in F003 each touch release / security posture across the repo, even though individually they look like 1-hour fixes. Operator review explicitly called out the anti-pattern: 'CI permissions, secret scanning regexes, Ruff S rules, SECURITY.md, and key-age warnings are small, but they touch release/security posture. Make them a small local plan.' Dropping them as drive-by edits inside other commits would mean (a) no auditor pass against the security framing (Ruff S as 'lint' not 'SAST'; SHA-pin without updater ≠ pin maintenance solved); (b) no decisions.jsonl record of why specific patterns were chosen vs others; (c) no documented deferral of the items NOT in scope (command_guard wiring, audit-log redaction, lockfile + pip-audit, supply-chain). Plan-level framing makes the commitments explicit and the deferrals defensible.
rationale: Locked-AC + scope-change-protocol memory: changes that cross posture boundaries get plans, even when each change is small.

question: Why is Ruff S not a full SAST and how do we frame it?
answer: Ruff S is a port of bandit's rule set — it covers in-tree code-pattern checks (subprocess shell=True, hardcoded passwords, weak crypto, pickle, eval, weak temp files, assert in non-test code). It does NOT cover (a) cross-file taint analysis (where input from one file flows to a sink in another), (b) framework-aware rules (SQL injection in Django ORM, XSS in template engines, etc.), (c) language-spanning analysis (TypeScript + Python in the same change), (d) custom rule packs against project-specific anti-patterns. Real SAST (semgrep with rule packs / CodeQL / Snyk Code) provides these. Calling Ruff S 'SAST' would over-claim coverage and create a false sense of completeness. F002 frames it as 'baseline security lint' in pyproject.toml, in SECURITY.md, and in any operator-facing doc. The phrase 'NOT a SAST substitute' is an explicit acceptance check (F002 #5).
rationale: Operator review: 'Ruff S is useful but not a full SAST substitute; phrase it as baseline security lint, not SAST solved.' Naming discipline prevents the next operator from skipping the real-SAST plan because they think the box is checked.

question: SHA-pinning maintenance tradeoff — Dependabot vs Renovate, and what happens if neither is wired?
answer: Default to Dependabot. Reason: (a) native to GitHub, zero external app install, zero operator overhead beyond merging the PRs; (b) coverage of `github-actions` + `pip` ecosystems is built-in; (c) simpler config (one YAML file). Renovate has more features (grouping, schedule windows, regex managers, etc.) but adds an external GitHub App with its own permissions surface. Jarvis is a single-operator tool today; Renovate's extras don't earn their complexity. SHA-pinning maintenance tradeoff: SHA pins prevent supply-chain attacks via tag-mutation (ad-hoc retag of `actions/checkout@v4` to malicious commit), but they require regular bot-merged updates or pins go stale (security patches don't reach the workflow). Without an updater bot, SHA pinning becomes a maintenance burden that operators forget — the worst of both worlds (manual work + stale pins). Therefore F003 ships SHA-pinning AND an updater config in the same feature; if Dependabot turns out unconfigurable in this slice (rare), F003 still ships pins but the rotation burden is operator-acknowledged in CONTRIBUTING.md. Operator review explicitly flagged this: 'SHA-pinning GitHub Actions is a tradeoff too: good security, higher maintenance unless Dependabot/Renovate updates pins.' D003 makes the bot a hard part of F003.
rationale: Either ship the maintenance story or don't pin. Pinning without rotation is theater.

question: Why are command_guard wiring + audit-log redaction explicitly out of scope here?
answer: Both are real platform-security gaps surfaced by the same research agent that identified F001-F003, but each carries enough design uncertainty to warrant its own plan rather than ride along here. (a) command_guard wiring: the research agent flagged that `claude_cli.py:67` and `codex_cli.py:75` call `subprocess.run` directly without invoking `command_guard.assert_allowed()`. Operator review correctly pushed back: 'Saying executors just don't call command_guard may be misleading. Claude/Codex CLIs execute tool calls internally; an outer Python wrapper may not see each Bash command unless the CLI exposes hooks/logs or the prompt contract requires command recording.' This is a design spike (item 6 in the corrected sequence v3), not a wiring fix. The spike memo answering 'is interception even possible?' must land before any implementation. (b) audit-log redaction: the gap is real (`DispatchResult.raw_response` is stored verbatim; an agent that runs `env | grep KEY` lands secrets in the audit chain), but a redaction layer carries false-positive risk — a regex that's too eager redacts legitimate audit content and breaks audit-integrity. Implementing it requires a test plan with synthetic positive + negative cases, which is a half-day plan with auditor review, not a baseline-hardening drive-by. Both are queued for follow-up plans.
rationale: Each gap that requires design before implementation is its own plan. This plan stays mechanical: regex additions, config edits, doc files, age check. No design uncertainty.

question: How do we keep sanitization_check.py from becoming a random regex pile over time?
answer: Every secret-shape regex added to sanitization_check.py must carry a code-comment citation to its public source — gitleaks default rules (https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks/blob/master/config/gitleaks.toml), vendor docs (https://docs.anthropic.com / etc.), or a tracked issue link. The 8 patterns added by F001 each get a `# source: <url>` comment immediately above the regex. Future PRs adding patterns must follow the same rule — D005 documents the policy so the next contributor doesn't drop in an undocumented regex. Rationale: operator review note 'add a source/evidence requirement for each secret pattern, so the scanner doesn't become a random regex pile.' Without a citation, regex review can't verify (a) the pattern is correct for the actual secret shape, (b) the pattern's false-positive rate is known, (c) whether a vendor has rotated the shape (e.g. Anthropic moved from `sk-...` to `sk-ant-...` in 2024). The citation makes the regex auditable.
rationale: Audit-friendly regex sources. No silent regex growth.

question: Tier choice — local vs cross-cutting?
answer: tier: local. Rationale: F001 + F002 are clearly local (single repo, no architectural changes, no cross-project shared schema bumps). F003 (SHA-pin + Dependabot) edits CI workflows and adds a bot config — affects every contributor's PR (Dependabot will open weekly PRs against `github-actions` updates that need merging). That edges toward 'cross-cutting' in the agent-conventions tier rubric, but the actual repo architecture doesn't change and there's no schema involved. Keeping the whole plan local keeps the audit pass tight. If F003 grows in scope (multiple ecosystems, custom Renovate rules, regex managers), bump to cross-cutting and re-audit.
rationale: Tier matches actual blast radius, not the loudness of the topic.

question: F002 first-wave stop rule — what protects against degenerating into a noisy mass-suppressions commit if Ruff S finds a lot?
answer: Hard threshold: if `ruff check --select S scripts/` produces >25 findings OR touches >8 distinct files, F002 STOPS at inventory and lands as `passes: false` with `signoff_reason: scope_split_required`. The inventory at `evidence/f002/ruff-s-first-wave-inventory.md` becomes input to a follow-up plan that handles bulk remediation as its own feature with its own auditor pass. Below the threshold, F002 proceeds with the per-finding fix-or-noqa-or-per-file-ignore policy. Rationale (operator review): without a stop rule, F002 could turn into a 50+-line noqa diff that makes the plan look like 'security' work while really just hiding findings. The plan should ENABLE the rule and clean the small amount of pre-existing dust, OR honestly report that the codebase has more dust than fits in one slice. Threshold values (25 findings / 8 files) are heuristics — small enough that one operator can review every suppression in a single sitting, large enough not to trip on a couple of test-file `assert` ignores.
rationale: Stop rules prevent compliance-theater outcomes where every finding gets a one-line excuse. If the codebase has too much dust, that's a separate plan, not a longer commit.

question: F002 stop-rule outcome — did the threshold trigger, and what's the follow-up shape?
answer: TRIGGERED HARD. `ruff check --select S scripts/` returned 853 findings across 30 distinct files. Both D007 thresholds blown (>25 findings AND >8 files). Per D007, F002 stopped at inventory: pyproject.toml NOT modified, SECURITY.md NOT extended, no per-file-ignores added. Rule breakdown: S101=810 (95%, `assert` in non-test code — overwhelmingly in scripts/jarvis_orchestrate/tests/), S108=15 (hardcoded /tmp), S603=14 (subprocess shell), S607=13 (start-process partial path), S310=1 (urlopen audit). The S101 wave is mostly false-positive: pytest USES assert as its assertion mechanism; the standard remediation is a one-line per-file-ignore for tests/** which drops 810→0. Post-ignore inventory expected ~43 findings — still over original threshold but small enough for per-finding remediation. Follow-up plan proposed: `feat-ruff-s-remediation` with two features: F001 = per-file-ignore baseline for tests/** (mechanical), F002 = per-finding remediation of residual ~43 non-test findings under fix/noqa/per-file-ignore policy. Both features carry the SECURITY.md 'baseline lint, NOT SAST' framing forward (D002 invariant). The follow-up plan opens after security plan F003 closes per corrected sequence v3 ordering. Stop-rule successfully prevented F002 from degenerating into a 853-line mass-suppressions commit — exactly the failure mode D007 was written against.
rationale: Stop rule worked as designed. The split into a follow-up plan keeps the audit pass tight per D001 (this is a plan, not opportunistic patch).

question: F003 review surfaced that the pip Dependabot promise was nonfunctional — the original 'manifest-update visibility ONLY' framing claimed bookkeeping that doesn't actually happen because Jarvis's pyproject.toml has no PEP 621 [project] table or requirements file. How is this resolved?
answer: Reframe pip ecosystem in dependabot.yml as **configured-but-no-op** rather than active visibility. Three reasons to keep the entry rather than remove it: (a) explicit intent — when a future dep-security plan adds a manifest, the bot activates automatically with no re-config step (one-line removal+re-add has the same effect but is less self-documenting); (b) honest framing — comment in the YAML + CONTRIBUTING.md state 'no-op until a manifest exists', so future readers don't assume it's doing supply-chain work; (c) audit clarity — D009 records the gap, F003 acceptance #4 matches reality. NOT chosen: (alt-A) remove pip entry — slightly cleaner but loses the bookkeeping intent record; (alt-B) add a PEP 621 [project] table to pyproject.toml — out of F003 scope because it changes Jarvis's packaging model from 'invoke as module' to 'pip-installable', which has implications across CONTRIBUTING.md install instructions, downstream consumers, the agent-conventions subtree, and bootstrap.sh. That packaging change belongs to the deferred dep-security plan that also owns hash-pinning + pip-audit + lockfile (D004 list). Acceptance #4 is updated to require both 'NOT dependency-security completion' AND 'NO-OP until a manifest exists' phrases in CONTRIBUTING.md; acceptance #5 adds 'PEP 621 [project] table' to the deferral list. Operator review surfaced the original framing as overclaiming; D009 corrects.
rationale: Original framing claimed coverage that doesn't exist. Reframing keeps the bookkeeping intent without overclaiming.

title: F003 acceptance #7 scope-change — pin correctness verified, latent CI debt deferred
body: Original acceptance #7 said 'CI runs green against the SHA-pinned actions on the next push'. After the SHA-pin push, three pre-existing CI failures surfaced in sequence: (1) ruff lint debt across 8 files (fixed in commit b6629b6); (2) bootstrap.sh dry-run requiring firebase CLI binary contrary to its own test's documented intent (fixed in commit 852d447); (3) jarvis_doctor --skip-auth failing on missing firebase CLI + missing target-project config in CI runner. Each failure was unrelated to F003's actual contract (SHA pin correctness + Dependabot updater policy). Per the operator-defined stop rule (after the third unrelated failure), F003 acceptance #7 is narrowed by scope-change to: 'the SHA-pinned actions execute correctly when CI runs, verified via run logs that show actions/checkout@<SHA> and actions/setup-python@<SHA> both running without errors before any downstream step fails.' Evidence: evidence/f003/post-pin-ci-run.md captures three CI runs all showing the SHA-pinned actions completing successfully. Why: the F003 contract was about pin correctness, not all-of-CI being green; expanding F003 to absorb general CI debt would (a) defeat the tight-boundary discipline and (b) keep growing as more debt surfaces. How to apply: the deferred CI debt (jarvis_doctor's firebase CLI presence + target-project resolution under --skip-auth) belongs to a future plan (proposed: feat-ci-baseline-cleanup) that addresses CI runner provisioning + jarvis_doctor's --skip-auth semantics holistically. Until that plan lands, CI on main is expected to fail at the doctor step on every push; this is documented in CONTRIBUTING.md as known-debt rather than treated as an F003 regression.
